lines.text: Welcome back. We've created the structure.
We've designed the appearance.
Now we need to teach the game what to do.
And we'll do it one behaviour at a time, straight down this list.
First, JavaScript needs to find our game pieces.
Remember the id name tags from the HTML video? This is why we made them.
get element by id means, go into the page, and find the thing called player.
We store it in a box called a variable, so we can use it later.
Let's check it worked. The console is JavaScript's notepad. And there's our player.
Next, we need the computer to know when the player presses Space.
add event listener means listen. Every time a key goes down, run this function.
If it's not the Space key, return. That means stop, and do nothing.
Press Space... and the console says, Space pressed. The game can hear us.
Now the jump.
Settings are numbers we choose. State is information that changes while you play. That's why it uses let. Let means the value can change.
A function is a set of instructions with a name. jump says, push the dinosaur upwards.
But games don't happen once. They happen over and over, like a flip book. That's the game loop.
request animation frame means, run me again on the next frame. About sixty times every second.
Let's try it.
Houston, we have a problem.
We pushed the dinosaur up, but nothing ever pulls it back down. The code is doing exactly what we told it. We just haven't told it about gravity.
One line of gravity.
Every frame, gravity takes a little bit off the upward speed. At the top, the speed is zero. Then it goes negative, and the dinosaur falls.
Better! But now, it doesn't know where the ground is.
So we add a landing check. If the dinosaur reaches the ground, put it on the ground, stop it moving, and let it jump again.
We ran it, saw a problem, figured out why, and fixed it. That's how real developers work.
Now the obstacle.
Every frame, the cactus moves six pixels to the left. When it disappears off the left edge, we send it back to the right, with a random gap.
And look. The ground scrolls, and the legs run. Remember those CSS animations? JavaScript just switched them on.
One small problem... our dinosaur is a ghost.
How does a computer see a crash? It doesn't. It compares boxes.
If the boxes overlap side to side, and up and down, they've crashed.
When you jump, they overlap side to side, but not up and down. So you're safe.
Run into the cactus, and everything stops. The game knows when we've crashed.
Score next. Every frame you survive, add a tenth of a point.
Math floor chops off the decimals, so the screen shows whole numbers.
Now, Game Over.
We already designed the crash look, and the Game Over screen, in CSS. JavaScript just flips the switches.
Add crashed, and the dinosaur turns red. Remove hidden, and Game Over appears.
Restart puts everything back to the beginning, and starts again.
Jump. Jump. Crash. Play again.
That's a working game. And you know what every line does, because you watched each one change something.
Now make it yours. Change the jump height. Change the speed. Try moon gravity. Change the obstacle. Turn it into your paper design.
Next time, we bring in Claude. And learn how to use AI to understand our code, fix problems, and add features.
